note: Short, predetermined scenarios for Mastery Blitz (Phase 5). Independently authored, general business situations, no DECA content. Each is 2-3 sentences and broad enough that any framework term can be applied to it in context. Picked at random per drill; the loop stays LLM-free.

scenarios.text: You're advising the owner of a neighborhood bakery. Foot traffic is down about 20% since a chain cafe opened two blocks away, the budget is tight, and the owner wants a plan for the next quarter.
You're the manager of a new boutique fitness studio opening downtown next month. You have one shot at a strong launch, a modest marketing budget, and a lot of established gyms nearby.
You're on the team at a consumer mobile app. Lots of people download it, but most stop using it within a week, and leadership wants that fixed before the next funding conversation.
You're advising a food-truck owner who's doing well and wants to add a second truck. Cash is limited, staff is stretched, and one bad decision could sink the whole business.
You manage a mid-size electronics store. Sales are steady but profit is slipping, and you suspect a mix of rising costs and inventory problems is to blame.

You're advising the owner of a hair salon whose online reviews have turned negative after a few bad experiences. New-client bookings have dropped and the owner is worried about the reputation spreading.
You work at a small nonprofit that relies on a handful of large donors. One major donor just pulled out, and you need a plan to stabilize funding without alienating the people you serve.
You're a founder about to launch a subscription software product for small businesses. You haven't set a price yet, competitors range widely, and you only get one first impression.
You manage a busy family restaurant losing servers faster than you can train them. Service quality is slipping, customers are noticing, and hiring season is competitive.
You're advising an online clothing boutique that wants to open its first physical store. Demand looks strong online, but a lease is a big fixed commitment and the team has never run a storefront.
You manage a coffee shop with lots of one-time visitors but few regulars. The owner wants more repeat business but is skeptical of spending on a complicated loyalty program.
You're the manager of a beach-town hotel heading into a slow off-season. Rooms will sit empty for months unless you find a way to fill them, and deep discounting could cheapen the brand.
You're advising a small manufacturer whose material costs just jumped. Raising prices risks losing key customers, but absorbing the increase would wipe out the margin on every unit.
You manage a neighborhood gym. A big-box fitness chain just opened nearby with lower prices and more equipment, and some of your members are already asking why they should stay.
You're advising an independent bookstore that wants to draw more people in. The owner has space for events and a small community following, but limited time and no dedicated marketing person.

You're on the team at a small juice brand about to put a new product on grocery shelves. Shelf space is competitive, the launch window is short, and first-week sales will shape whether stores keep carrying it.
